# Network Visualization with cograph: A Complete Plotting Guide

## 1 Introduction

Network visualization in R has traditionally meant choosing between two
extremes: quick-and-dirty plots that look like hairballs, or heavily
customized code that takes longer to write than the analysis itself.
**cograph** collapses this tradeoff. The
[`splot()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md) function
produces publication-ready network visualizations from a single call,
with sensible defaults that you can override parameter by parameter.

This tutorial demonstrates everything through a single TNA model of
collaborative regulation behaviors. We start with a zero-argument plot
and progressively layer in customization — so you can see exactly what
each parameter changes.

1.  **The plot** — one line, zero arguments, publication-ready
2.  **Node styling** — shapes, colors, sizes, labels, centrality-based
    scaling
3.  **Edge styling** — width, color, curvature, labels, thresholds
4.  **Donuts and pies** — composite node shapes for multivariate data
5.  **Themes and palettes** — pre-built visual themes
6.  **Pipe-friendly API** — the `sn_*` function family for chainable
    plot building
7.  **Specialized plots** — chord diagrams, heatmaps, alluvial flows
8.  **Group comparisons** — difference networks and multi-group grids
9.  **Bootstrap** — validated network visualization
10. **Permutation testing** — significant group differences
11. **Mixed networks** — directed and undirected edges combined

For TNA-specific workflows, see the [TNA
tutorial](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/articles/plotting-tna-models.md).

> **GitHub Development Version**
>
> This tutorial covers the full feature set available in the **GitHub
> development version** of cograph. The CRAN release provides the core
> plotting engine; the development version adds themes, pipe API,
> specialized plots, and additional features.
>
> ``` r
>
> # Development version with full features
> # devtools::install_github("sonsoleslp/cograph")
> # CRAN version
> install.packages("cograph")
> ```

## 2 Building the Model

We use the built-in `group_regulation` dataset from the `tna` package —
coded collaborative regulation behaviors from student groups. This gives
us a 9-state directed transition network, the kind of rich structure
that showcases cograph’s capabilities.

``` r

library(tna)
data("group_regulation")
model <- tna(group_regulation)
model
```

We also prepare a group model for later comparison and permutation
sections:

``` r

data("group_regulation_long")
prepared <- prepare_data(group_regulation_long,
                         action = "Action", actor = "Actor", time = "Time")
group_model <- group_tna(prepared, group = "Achiever")
```

## 3 The Plot

One function. Zero arguments beyond the model. Publication-ready.

``` r

splot(model)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1: splot(model) — that’s it

When cograph receives a TNA object, it auto-applies TNA-appropriate
defaults: oval layout, dark blue edges weighted by transition
probability, donut rings showing initial state probabilities, and
directional arrows. Every aspect of this plot can be customized — the
rest of this tutorial shows how.

## 4 Node Styling

### 4.1 Shapes

Every node can have its own shape. cograph supports circles, squares,
hexagons, diamonds, triangles, pentagons, stars, hearts, and more:

``` r

splot(model,
  node_shape = c("circle", "square", "hexagon", "diamond", "triangle",
                 "pentagon", "star", "heart", "circle"),
  layout = "circle"
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 2: Different shapes per node

> **All Built-In Shapes**
>
> `"circle"`, `"square"`, `"triangle"`, `"diamond"`, `"pentagon"`,
> `"hexagon"`, `"star"`, `"heart"`, `"ellipse"`, `"cross"`,
> `"rectangle"`, `"pie"`, `"donut"`
>
> You can also register **custom SVG shapes** with
> [`register_svg_shape()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/shapes.md)
> and use them by name.

### 4.2 Colors and Sizes

``` r

splot(model,
  node_fill = palette_viridis(9),
  node_border_color = "white",
  node_border_width = 2,
  node_size = c(12, 8, 10, 9, 7, 11, 8, 10, 9)
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3: Custom fills, borders, and per-node sizes

### 4.3 Shortening Long Labels

Use `label_abbrev` when full node names crowd the plot. It follows the
same convention as
[`plot_mcml()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/plot_mcml.md):
`NULL` keeps full labels, an integer sets a fixed maximum length, and
`"auto"` chooses a maximum from the number of nodes. Shortened labels
end with an ellipsis, which is included in the maximum length.

``` r

long_labels <- c(
  "Orientation", "Planning", "Reading", "Watching", "Trying",
  "Reviewing", "Reflection", "Submission", "Revision"
)
splot(model, labels = long_labels, label_abbrev = 4)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 4: Node labels abbreviated to at most four characters

### 4.4 Scaling Nodes by Centrality

`scale_nodes_by` maps a centrality measure to node size — larger nodes
are more central. This is one of the most useful parameters for making
network structure immediately visible:

``` r

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
splot(model, scale_nodes_by = "betweenness", node_size_range = c(3, 14),
      title = "Betweenness")
splot(model, scale_nodes_by = "strength", node_size_range = c(3, 14),
      title = "Strength")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 5: Node size proportional to different centrality measures

> **scale_nodes_by Options**
>
> Any centrality measure name works: `"degree"`, `"strength"`,
> `"betweenness"`, `"closeness"`, `"eigenvector"`, `"pagerank"`,
> `"authority"`, `"hub"`, `"eccentricity"`, `"coreness"`,
> `"constraint"`, `"transitivity"`, `"harmonic"`, `"diffusion"`,
> `"leverage"`, `"kreach"`.
>
> For directional measures (in/out), use a list:
> `scale_nodes_by = list("strength", mode = "in")`.
>
> | Parameter         | Default   | Description                               |
> |-------------------|-----------|-------------------------------------------|
> | `scale_nodes_by`  | `NULL`    | Centrality measure name or list with mode |
> | `node_size_range` | `c(2, 8)` | `c(min, max)` size range for mapping      |

## 5 Edge Styling

### 5.1 Width and Curvature

``` r

splot(model,
  edge_width = 3,
  curvature = 0.3,
  arrow_size = 0.015
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 6: Custom edge width range with curvature

### 5.2 Edge Labels

Display transition probabilities directly on edges:

``` r

splot(model,
  edge_labels = TRUE,
  edge_label_size = 0.6,
  edge_label_bg = "white",
  threshold = 0.05
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 7: Edge labels showing transition weights

### 5.3 Thresholding

Hide weak transitions to reveal the backbone:

``` r

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
splot(model, title = "All edges")
splot(model, threshold = 0.10, title = "threshold = 0.10")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 8: Thresholding removes visual clutter

> **Edge Parameters**
>
> | Parameter             | Default   | Description                            |
> |-----------------------|-----------|----------------------------------------|
> | `edge_width`          | auto      | Base edge width                        |
> | `edge_width_range`    | auto      | `c(min, max)` width range              |
> | `edge_color`          | auto      | Edge color                             |
> | `edge_alpha`          | `1`       | Transparency                           |
> | `edge_style`          | `"solid"` | `"solid"`, `"dashed"`, `"dotted"`      |
> | `curvature`           | auto      | Curve amount                           |
> | `arrow_size`          | auto      | Arrowhead size                         |
> | `threshold`           | `0`       | Hide edges below this weight           |
> | `edge_labels`         | `FALSE`   | Show weight labels                     |
> | `edge_label_style`    | `"plain"` | `"plain"`, `"ci"`, `"stars"`, `"full"` |
> | `edge_positive_color` | auto      | Color for positive weights             |
> | `edge_negative_color` | auto      | Color for negative weights             |

## 6 Donuts and Pies

Donut and pie node shapes encode **additional quantitative information**
directly in the node rendering. In TNA, the donut ring is automatically
filled from initial state probabilities — but you can use it for any
node-level metric.

### 6.1 Donut Nodes

The default TNA plot already shows donut fills from `model$inits`. You
can customize the appearance:

``` r

splot(model, 
      donut_color = "black",
      donut_bg_color = "white",
      donut_border_color = "black",
      donut_shape = "circle"
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 9: Donuts with custom styling

### 6.2 Pie Nodes

Pie chart nodes show a categorical distribution per node. You can
combine them with the outer donut ring:

``` r

# Each node gets a 3-slice pie (e.g., from a clustering or condition split)
pie_vals <- list(
  c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2), c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2), c(0.3, 0.3, 0.4),
  c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2), c(0.2, 0.5, 0.3), c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3),
  c(0.7, 0.2, 0.1), c(0.3, 0.4, 0.3), c(0.5, 0.2, 0.3)
)

splot(model,
  pie_values = pie_vals,
  pie_colors = c("#1976D2", "#FFA000", "#C62828"),
  layout = "circle"
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 10: Donut ring (initial probability) + inner pie segments

> **Donut & Pie Parameters**
>
> | Parameter | Default | Description |
> |----|----|----|
> | `donut_fill` | auto (from TNA inits) | Numeric 0–1 per node |
> | `donut_color` | auto | Fill color for the ring |
> | `donut_inner_ratio` | `0.5` | Inner radius ratio (0–1) |
> | `donut_shape` | `"circle"` | `"circle"`, `"square"`, `"hexagon"`, `"diamond"`, `"triangle"`, `"pentagon"` |
> | `donut_show_value` | `FALSE` | Show numeric value in center |
> | `donut_value_suffix` | `""` | Text after value (e.g., `"%"`) |
> | `pie_values` | `NULL` | List of numeric vectors per node |
> | `pie_colors` | auto | Colors for pie segments |

## 7 Themes and Palettes

Themes apply a coordinated set of visual defaults with a single
parameter:

``` r

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
splot(model, theme = "classic",    title = "classic")
splot(model, theme = "dark",       title = "dark")
splot(model, theme = "minimal",    title = "minimal")
splot(model, theme = "colorblind", title = "colorblind")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 11: Four built-in themes

``` r

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
splot(model, node_fill = palette_viridis(9),    title = "viridis")
splot(model, node_fill = palette_pastel(9),     title = "pastel")
splot(model, node_fill = palette_colorblind(9), title = "colorblind")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 12: Color palettes for nodes

> **All Themes**
>
> | Theme          | Description                     |
> |----------------|---------------------------------|
> | `"classic"`    | Clean, professional (default)   |
> | `"dark"`       | Dark background, light elements |
> | `"minimal"`    | Reduced chrome, subtle colors   |
> | `"colorblind"` | Colorblind-safe palette         |
> | `"grayscale"`  | No color, grayscale only        |
> | `"vibrant"`    | Bold, saturated colors          |
> | `"nature"`     | Earth-tone palette              |
> | `"viridis"`    | Viridis color scale             |
>
> Use [`list_themes()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/themes.md)
> to see all registered themes. Create custom themes with
> [`register_theme()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/themes.md).

## 8 Pipe-Friendly API (ggplot2)

The `sn_*` function family lets you build plots incrementally using the
pipe operator. Each function takes a cograph_network and returns a
modified one:

``` r

model |>
  cograph(layout = "circle") |>
  sn_theme("dark") |>
  sn_nodes(size = 10, shape = "hexagon",
           border_color = "white", border_width = 2) |>
  sn_edges(width = 4, curvature = 0.2) |>
  soplot(title = "Built with pipes")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 13: Dark-themed hexagon network built with pipes

> **All sn\_\* Functions**
>
> | Function | What It Configures |
> |----|----|
> | `sn_layout(network, layout, seed)` | Layout algorithm |
> | `sn_theme(network, theme)` | Visual theme |
> | `sn_palette(network, palette, target, by)` | Color palette for nodes or edges |
> | `sn_nodes(network, ...)` | All node aesthetics (size, shape, fill, labels, pie, donut) |
> | `sn_edges(network, ...)` | All edge aesthetics (width, color, labels, curvature, CI) |
> | `sn_render(network, ...)` | Render with grid graphics (alias for [`soplot()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/soplot.md)) |
> | `sn_ggplot(network, title)` | Convert to ggplot2 object |
> | `sn_save(network, filename, ...)` | Save to file (PDF/PNG/SVG) |

## 9 Specialized Plots

### 9.1 Chord Diagram

Chord diagrams show flows as curved ribbons around a circle. The width
of each ribbon is proportional to the transition weight:

``` r

plot_chord(model, chord_alpha = 0.6, title = "Transition Flows")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 14: Chord diagram of transition flows

> **Chord Diagram Parameters**
>
> | Parameter | Default | Description |
> |----|----|----|
> | `segment_colors` | auto | Colors for each node’s arc |
> | `chord_color_by` | `"source"` | Color ribbons by `"source"`, `"target"`, or `"weight"` |
> | `chord_alpha` | `0.5` | Ribbon transparency |
> | `self_loop` | `FALSE` | Show self-transition arcs? |
> | `threshold` | `0` | Hide chords below this weight |

### 9.2 Heatmap

The adjacency matrix as a color-coded grid, optionally grouped by
cluster:

``` r

clusters <- list(
  Social    = c("discuss", "consensus", "cohesion", "emotion"),
  Cognitive = c("plan", "monitor", "adapt", "synthesis"),
  Meta      = c("coregulate")
)

plot_heatmap(model,
  cluster_list = clusters,
  show_values = TRUE,
  value_size = 3.5,
  title = "Transition Heatmap"
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 15: Transition heatmap with clustered groups

### 9.3 Alluvial / Sankey Diagram

Shows source-to-target flow as an alluvial diagram:

``` r

plot_alluvial(model$weights, threshold = 0.05)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 16: Alluvial diagram of transition flows

## 10 Group Comparisons

### 10.1 Multi-Group Grid

When you pass a `group_tna` object, splot renders all groups in a grid:

``` r

splot(group_model, i = NULL)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 17: High vs Low achiever networks side by side

### 10.2 Difference Network

[`plot_compare()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/plot_compare.md)
computes and visualizes the element-wise difference between two groups.
Green edges are stronger in the first group; red edges are stronger in
the second:

``` r

plot_compare(group_model,
  pos_color = "#2A9D8F",
  neg_color = "#E76F51",
  title = "High vs Low"
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 18: Difference network: High - Low achievers

## 11 Bootstrap

The bootstrap procedure determines which edges are stable properties of
the data and which are sampling artifacts. Pass a `tna_bootstrap` object
to [`splot()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md) and it
automatically styles significant vs. non-significant edges:

``` r

set.seed(265)
boot <- bootstrap(model, iter = 1000, level = 0.05)
```

``` r

splot(boot)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 19: Bootstrap-validated network (solid = significant, dashed =
non-significant)

``` r

splot(boot, display = "significant")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 20: Only significant edges shown

``` r

splot(boot, display = "ci", threshold = 0.05)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 21: Confidence interval labels on edges

> **Bootstrap Display Modes**
>
> | `display`            | Description                                   |
> |----------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
> | `"styled"` (default) | Significant = solid, non-significant = dashed |
> | `"significant"`      | Only significant edges shown                  |
> | `"full"`             | All edges shown with equal styling            |
> | `"ci"`               | Confidence interval labels on edges           |
>
> Additional parameters: `show_stars` (significance stars), `show_ci`
> (CI values), `width_by` (scale width by weight or CI width).

## 12 Permutation Testing

Permutation testing evaluates whether between-group differences are
statistically significant. Pass the result to
[`splot()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md) to visualize
which edge differences survived the permutation test:

``` r

set.seed(265)
perm <- tna::permutation_test(group_model, iter = 1000)
```

``` r

splot(perm)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 22: Permutation test: significant between-group edge differences

> **Permutation Plot Parameters**
>
> | Parameter           | Default    | Description                            |
> |---------------------|------------|----------------------------------------|
> | `show_nonsig`       | `TRUE`     | Show non-significant edges?            |
> | `edge_nonsig_color` | `"gray80"` | Color for non-significant edges        |
> | `edge_nonsig_alpha` | `0.3`      | Transparency for non-significant edges |
> | `show_stars`        | `FALSE`    | Show significance stars                |
> | `show_effect`       | `FALSE`    | Show effect sizes                      |

## 13 Mixed Networks

Overlay directed and undirected edges on the same plot. This is useful
when you have two types of relationships — for example, symmetric
co-occurrence patterns and asymmetric transition probabilities. The
defaults follow TNA conventions: oval layout, weight-scaled edges,
dotted edge starts, and visible edge labels.

``` r

# Undirected: symmetric co-occurrence (half the weight for visual balance)
set.seed(42)
sym <- (model$weights + t(model$weights)) / 2
noise <- matrix(runif(length(sym), -0.02, 0.02), nrow = nrow(sym))
noise <- (noise + t(noise)) / 2  # keep symmetric
diag(noise) <- 0
sym <- pmax(sym * 0.5 + noise, 0)

# Directed: original transition probabilities
asym <- model$weights

# Defaults: oval layout, blue edges, weight-scaled widths, edge labels
plot_mixed_network(sym, asym, threshold = 0.03,
  title = "Co-occurrence + Transitions"
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 23: Co-occurrence (steel blue, straight) and transitions (dark
blue, curved) with TNA-style defaults

You can distinguish edge types by color: undirected co-occurrence edges
are straight steel-blue lines, while directed transitions are curved
dark-blue arrows with dotted starts. Edge widths scale automatically by
weight, so stronger connections stand out.

``` r

plot_mixed_network(sym, asym, threshold = 0.03,
  sym_color = "#E63946",
  asym_color = "#003355",
  title = "Red undirected + Blue directed"
)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 24: Custom colors to visually separate edge types

## 14 Multi-Cluster Visualization

[`plot_mcml()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/plot_mcml.md)
draws two layers simultaneously: individual nodes inside cluster shells
(bottom) and aggregated cluster-level summary pies (top).

``` r

clusters <- list(
  Social    = c("discuss", "consensus", "cohesion", "emotion"),
  Cognitive = c("plan", "monitor", "adapt", "synthesis"),
  Meta      = c("coregulate")
)

mat <- model$weights

plot_mcml(mat, clusters, mode = "tna",
  title = "Collaborative Regulation Clusters")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 25: Two-layer hierarchical cluster view

[`plot_mtna()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/plot_mtna.md)
provides a flat single-layer alternative:

``` r

plot_mtna(mat, clusters, show_labels = TRUE, label_abbrev = 4,
  title = "Flat Cluster Map")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 26: Flat cluster layout

## 15 Nestimate Integration

The **Nestimate** package estimates networks from sequence data using
multiple methods. Its objects dispatch through
[`splot()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md)
automatically.

``` r

library(Nestimate)

net <- build_network(group_regulation, method = "relative")
splot(net, title = "Nestimate: relative transitions")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Bootstrap stability:

``` r

set.seed(42)
nboot <- bootstrap_network(net, iter = 500)
splot(nboot, title = "Nestimate bootstrap")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Group comparison:

``` r

grp <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "relative",
  action = "Action", actor = "Actor", time = "Time",
  group = "Achiever")
splot(grp)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## 16 Motifs

Motif analysis identifies recurring local connectivity patterns — the
building blocks of network structure. The unified
[`motifs()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/motifs.md) and
[`subgraphs()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/subgraphs.md) APIs
use the MAN (Mutual, Asymmetric, Null) classification for directed
triads: 16 possible patterns from empty (003) to fully connected (300).
For the separate four-class undirected census, use
`motif_census(..., directed = FALSE)`.

### 16.1 Census

[`motifs()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/motifs.md) counts how
often each MAN type appears and tests significance against a
configuration-model null. The null depends on the analysis level:
aggregate matrices use loop-free simple-graph degree-preserving
rewiring, whereas individual transition data use target-stub shuffling
with integerized in/out margins followed by a loopless simple
projection. These are intentionally different reference models. Repeated
states (A → A) are removed before counting and before the null;
`count_repeats = TRUE` counts them toward `min_transitions` and shuffles
them with the other transitions, which suits coded data where one code
covers distinct events. With `p_adjust`, the `sig` column and the plot
colours use the adjusted p-values.

``` r

mot <- motifs(model, significance = TRUE, n_perm = 100, seed = 42)
mot
```

    Motif Census

    Significance: permutation (n_perm=100)

    Type distribution:
    120C 030C 030T  210 120U 120D  300
    1481 1044  620  581  190  178   79

    Top 7 results:
     type count expected     z          p      p_adj   sig
     120C  1481  1036.21 16.33 0.00990099 0.00990099  TRUE
     030T   620   423.69  7.95 0.00990099 0.00990099  TRUE
     120U   190   138.75  4.83 0.00990099 0.00990099  TRUE
      210   581   475.27  4.71 0.00990099 0.00990099  TRUE
     120D   178   139.20  3.82 0.00990099 0.00990099  TRUE
     030C  1044  1089.58 -1.46 0.17821782 0.17821782 FALSE
      300    79    81.53 -0.25 0.81188119 0.81188119 FALSE

The default `edge_method = "any"` is the fully supported inferential
path. For aggregate input with `edge_method = "expected"` or
`"percent"`, observed counts are thresholded but significance tests the
unthresholded network and emits a warning. In individual census mode the
threshold is reapplied to each integerized null replicate; positive
fractional weights still retain at least one stub, so mass-sensitive
inference can differ from the original fractional scale. In individual
named-instance mode, the optimized null classifies raw stub presence
rather than reapplying the non-`"any"` threshold. Descriptive calls with
`significance = FALSE` use the requested edge method directly.

For `edge_method = "percent"`, an edge is compared with the total weight
of the six possible directed edges inside its node triple—not with all
outgoing transitions from one node. Values at or below 1 are
proportions; values above 1 are percentages.

### 16.2 Visualization

``` r

plot(mot, type = "significance")
```

``` r

plot(mot, type = "patterns")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 28: MAN triad pattern diagrams

### 16.3 Named subgraphs

[`subgraphs()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/subgraphs.md)
identifies the specific node triples forming each pattern — which states
participate in which motifs. By default (`strict = TRUE`) each row is
one node triple with one exact set of arrows, so a cycle and its reverse
are separate rows, and at individual level `observed` counts the
sessions in which the triple shows exactly those arrows. A triple can
therefore appear in several rows. `strict = FALSE` pools the arrow
patterns of each MAN type into one row per `(node triple, MAN type)`.

``` r

sg <- subgraphs(model, significance = TRUE, top = 10,
  pattern = "triangle", seed = 42)
sg
```

Each panel draws the arrows of its row, with `node1` at the top, `node2`
bottom left and `node3` bottom right, so the diagram shows which state
leads to which. With `strict = FALSE` it draws the most frequent pattern
of the row, and the caption says how many sessions match the drawing
when the row pools other patterns.

## 17 Higher-Order Networks

Standard TNA assumes first-order Markov dynamics: the next state depends
only on the current state. Higher-order analysis tests whether longer
sequential memory exists — cases where what happened two or three steps
ago changes the transition probabilities.

### 17.1 Model order selection

[`build_mogen()`](https://pak.dynasite.org/Nestimate/reference/build_mogen.html)
fits Markov models at increasing orders and selects the best via
AIC/BIC:

``` r

data("human_long", package = "Nestimate")
hon_net <- build_network(human_long, method = "tna",
  action = "code", time = "timestamp", session = "session_id")
```

``` r

mg <- build_mogen(hon_net, max_order = 4)
summary(mg)
```

### 17.2 Higher-Order Network (HON)

HON detects *where* in the state space higher-order dependencies exist —
which transitions change depending on prior context:

``` r

hon <- build_hon(hon_net)
hon
```

    Higher-Order Network (HON)
      Nodes:        977 (9 first-order states)
      Edges:        3733
      Max order:    5 (requested 5)
      Min freq:     1
      Trajectories: 508

### 17.3 Path anomaly detection (HYPA)

HYPA identifies paths that occur significantly more or less often than
expected under a hypergeometric null model:

``` r

hypa <- build_hypa(hon_net)
table(hypa$scores$anomaly)
```


    normal   over  under
       525    133     44 

Over-represented paths — learned behavioral routines:

``` r

over <- subset(hypa$scores, anomaly == "over")
```

### 17.4 Simplicial visualization

[`plot_simplicial()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/plot_simplicial.md)
renders higher-order pathways as smooth blobs over the network. Source
states appear in blue, target states in red.

``` r

plot_simplicial(hon_net, max_pathways = 6,
  title = "Higher-Order Pathways")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 31: Top 6 higher-order pathways (HON)

Dismantled view — one panel per pathway:

``` r

plot_simplicial(hon_net, max_pathways = 9,
  dismantled = TRUE, ncol = 3)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 32: Individual pathway panels

HYPA anomalous pathways:

``` r

plot_simplicial(hon_net, method = "hypa", max_pathways = 9,
  dismantled = TRUE, ncol = 3)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 33: Anomalous pathways detected by HYPA

## 18 Robustness

[`robustness()`](https://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/robustness.md)
simulates network degradation under targeted and random node/edge
removal:

``` r

plot_robustness(x = mat,
  measures = c("betweenness", "degree", "random"),
  n_iter = 50, seed = 42,
  title = "Node Removal Robustness")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 34: Network robustness under targeted and random node removal

## 19 Saving and Exporting

### 19.1 Direct File Output

``` r

# Save as PNG
splot(model, filename = "network.png", width = 8, height = 8, res = 300)

# Save as PDF
splot(model, filename = "network.pdf", width = 8, height = 8)

# Save as SVG
splot(model, filename = "network.svg", width = 8, height = 8)
```

### 19.2 Pipe-Friendly Saving

``` r

model |>
  cograph(layout = "circle") |>
  sn_theme("dark") |>
  sn_nodes(size = 10) |>
  sn_save("network_dark.png", width = 8, height = 8, dpi = 300)
```

### 19.3 ggplot2 Export

``` r

p <- model |>
  cograph(layout = "circle") |>
  sn_ggplot()

ggplot2::ggsave("network.pdf", p, width = 8, height = 8)
```

## 20 Selected Parameter Reference

> **splot() — Selected Parameters**
>
> **Input & Layout:** `x`, `layout`, `directed`, `seed`, `theme`,
> `title`, `background`, `groups`
>
> **Node Appearance:** `node_size`, `node_size2`, `node_shape`,
> `node_fill`, `node_border_color`, `node_border_width`, `node_alpha`,
> `scale_nodes_by`, `node_size_range`
>
> **Labels:** `labels`, `label_abbrev`, `label_size`, `label_color`,
> `label_position`, `label_fontface`, `label_fontfamily`
>
> **Donut:** `donut_fill`, `donut_color`, `donut_inner_ratio`,
> `donut_shape`, `donut_show_value`, `donut_value_suffix`,
> `donut_value_digits`, `donut2_values`, `donut2_colors`
>
> **Pie:** `pie_values`, `pie_colors`
>
> **Edge Appearance:** `edge_color`, `edge_width`, `edge_size`,
> `edge_width_range`, `edge_scale_mode`, `edge_cutoff`, `edge_alpha`,
> `edge_style`, `edge_start_style`, `edge_positive_color`,
> `edge_negative_color`, `curvature`, `curves`
>
> **Arrows:** `arrow_size`, `arrow_angle`, `show_arrows`,
> `bidirectional`
>
> **Edge Labels:** `edge_labels`, `edge_label_size`, `edge_label_color`,
> `edge_label_bg`, `edge_label_position`, `edge_label_offset`,
> `edge_label_fontface`, `edge_label_style`, `edge_label_template`
>
> **CI Underlay:** `edge_ci`, `edge_ci_scale`, `edge_ci_alpha`,
> `edge_ci_color`, `edge_ci_style`
>
> **Weight / Threshold:** `threshold`, `minimum`, `maximum`,
> `weight_digits`
>
> **Layout Control:** `rescale`, `layout_scale`, `layout_margin`,
> `aspect`, `loop_rotation`
>
> **File Output:** `filename`, `filetype`, `width`, `height`, `res`
>
> **TNA:** `i` (group index for group_tna)

> **All Available Layouts**
>
> **Built-in:** `"oval"` (default), `"circle"`, `"spring"`, `"grid"`,
> `"random"`, `"star"`, `"bipartite"`, `"groups"`
>
> **igraph (two-letter codes):** `"kk"` (Kamada-Kawai), `"fr"`
> (Fruchterman-Reingold), `"drl"`, `"mds"`, `"lgl"`, `"ni"` (nicely),
> `"tr"` (tree), `"st"` (Sugiyama)
>
> You can also pass a **custom layout matrix** (2-column matrix with x,
> y coordinates) or a **layout function**.
